content: The data from three out of eight head-to-head studies was derived from a non-random selection of study populations that did not receive preventive therapy. This limits the ability to generalize the findings to other settings with confidence. There is a likely risk of bias, and publication bias was not formally assessed but is expected to be probable. Several large prospective studies are ongoing, but their results were not included in this analysis. However, the inclusion of these results is not anticipated to alter the overall conclusions of this review. The ascertainment of tuberculosis (TB) varied across the three studies. One study relied on passive follow-up with database linkage (Leung 2008), another used active follow-up but relied on self-reported data from participants (Shanaube 2013, unpublished), and the third incorporated active follow-up with the inclusion of tuberculin skin test (TST) and interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) results in the case definition (Mahommed 2011). The study populations analyzed were diverse, including a cohort with silicosis in China, adolescents in South Africa, and TB close contacts in Zambia or South Africa. The cut-offs for a positive TST result varied between studies, with two studies using a 10 mm threshold and one using a 5 mm threshold. Two of the three studies employed the QuantiFERON-TB Gold In-Tube (QFT-GIT) as the commercial IGRA, while the third used the T-SPOT.TB assay. Although the incidence rate ratios (IRRs) were relatively consistent across studies and the heterogeneity of the pooled IRR estimate was low, caution is advised when generalizing these results to other populations or settings. Publication bias was not formally assessed but is expected to be likely. Several large prospective studies are ongoing, and their results were not included in this analysis. However, the addition of these results is not expected to change the overall conclusions of this review. Heterogeneity was high for the pooled relative risk (RR) estimates for both TST and commercial IGRA. All three studies were conducted in countries with high or intermediate TB prevalence, and the pooled estimate is based on only three studies. Immunocompromised individuals who did not receive preventive therapy may not be representative of all immunocompromised individuals. There is very serious imprecision in the RR estimates for both TST and IGRA. One study included in the analysis had limited external validity, meaning its findings may not be generalizable to other populations. Another study included a limited number of events, resulting in very wide confidence intervals around the IRR estimate. Publication bias was not formally assessed but is expected to be likely. Heterogeneity was very high (86%) for the pooled RR estimate for the commercial IGRA. The analysis was based on a small number of studies with varying definitions of case contact. Two studies were conducted in low-prevalence countries, and one study was conducted in a high-prevalence country. Despite the lack of heterogeneity, there is concern that TB case contacts in these three studies may not be representative of all TB case contacts. The GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) system was used to assess the certainty of evidence. High-certainty evidence indicates a very good indication of the likely effect, with a low likelihood of substantial differences. Moderate-certainty evidence provides a good indication of the likely effect, with a moderate likelihood of substantial differences. Low-certainty evidence offers some indication of the likely effect, but the likelihood of substantial differences is high. Very low-certainty evidence does not provide a reliable indication of the likely effect, with a very high likelihood of substantial differences. The treatment of latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI) aims to prevent the progression of asymptomatic TB infection to clinically active TB disease. Effective treatment is a critical component of the programmatic management of LTBI. The choice of the most appropriate treatment regimen should be based on evidence regarding efficacy, tolerability, acceptability, costs, feasibility under programmatic conditions, and the risk of fostering drug resistance during treatment. Safety is particularly important in the context of LTBI treatment, as all treated patients are healthy, and only a small minority would develop active TB even without treatment. With currently used anti-TB drugs, safety concerns are primarily related to hepatotoxicity. For example, the widely used drug isoniazid can cause liver-related side effects, including toxic hepatitis of grade II and IV severity and, in rare cases, death. LTBI treatment can prevent 60-90% of reactivation TB cases. Isoniazid alone, administered daily at a dose of 5 mg/kg (up to 300 mg/day) for six months, has been a mainstay of treatment for a long time. Other regimens have also been considered, including daily rifampicin alone (for 3 or 4 months), daily isoniazid and rifampicin (for 3 months), daily rifampicin and pyrazinamide (for 2 months), daily isoniazid, rifampicin, and pyrazinamide (for 3 months), and isoniazid (900 mg) and rifapentine (900 mg) given once weekly for 12 weeks. Many randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of LTBI treatment have been conducted, although not all regimens have been directly compared with a placebo. One of the obstacles to widespread implementation of LTBI treatment is the concern that prophylaxis may increase resistance to the specific drug used for preventive therapy. It is therefore important to investigate this issue and, if possible, address the concern. A systematic review was conducted to determine whether LTBI treatment leads to significant development of resistance against the drugs used. The review found that LTBI treatment with 6 to 12 months of isoniazid did not lead to a significant increase in resistance to isoniazid, and preventive treatment with rifamycin-containing regimens did not significantly increase rifamycin resistance. However, there was insufficient evidence on the incidence of isoniazid resistance in HIV-infected individuals receiving continuous isoniazid. The quality of evidence for these findings ranged from very low to moderate. The choice of LTBI treatment regimen should also consider cost-effectiveness. For example, 6 months of isoniazid (6H) versus 9 months of isoniazid (9H) may result in small cost savings, while rifampicin (RMP) versus 6H may also result in small savings. However, the incremental cost relative to the net benefit varies depending on the regimen and the specific context.
